blocks.text: The chapter moves from waiting for an answer to a written vision and then to a series of five “woes”—pronouncements of judgment. These woes address plunder, exploitative gain, blood-built cities, humiliating violence, and idols. Together they portray the reversal of a proud aggressor: what has been taken by violence will be turned back against the taker.

The opening scene presents the speaker at a watchpost, awaiting God’s response and prepared to receive correction. The answer is to write the vision plainly: it has an appointed time, so apparent delay calls for waiting. Verse 4 then contrasts a swollen or crooked figure with the righteous person who lives by emunah. This Hebrew term can convey firmness, fidelity, faithfulness, or faith, so translations differ over how best to express the contrast.

Romans 1:16–17 later links its account of God’s righteousness and the gospel’s saving power to Habakkuk 2:4. That later use makes this verse especially important for readers of both books, though the precise sense of Romans’s phrase “from faith to faith” and the identity of Habakkuk’s speaker remain debated.

sections.title: Waiting, Living, and a Difficult Phrase

blocks.text: The woes connect unjust gain and city-building with bloodshed, futile labor, and eventual shame. Royal inscriptions from Nabopolassar and Nebuchadnezzar II offer a relevant backdrop: they celebrate piety, construction, fortification, labor, and justice, while also presenting an ideological royal self-portrait. Habakkuk’s language of houses, walls, beams, and blood-built cities exposes how impressive building and security can be implicated in exploitation.

Several images sharpen the chapter’s portrayal of reversal. The first woe uses difficult wordplay involving pledges, debtors, or “biters,” but its direction is clear: those who plunder others become plunder themselves. The fourth woe uses forced drinking, exposure, and the cup of Jehovah’s right hand to depict the violent aggressor’s humiliation. Verse 17 also joins violence against Lebanon and animals to violence against lands, cities, and inhabitants; this can support an ecological reading, though it does not exhaust the verse’s meaning.

Against labor that ends in fire and futility, verse 14 envisions the earth filled with knowledge of Jehovah’s glory as waters cover the sea. The final woe contrasts crafted, speechless idols with Jehovah in the holy temple, before calling the whole earth to silence. The chapter therefore closes by setting human pride and powerless images against Jehovah’s presence and glory.
